lines.t: Ridgewatch is a camp of patched canvas pitched in the lee of a broken wall. Cookfires burn low, and every tent faces north, toward the ridge.
Above the camp, black against the grey sky, the old Dawn chapel squats on its hilltop. A gallows has been raised on the roof, and something swings from it in the wind.
A sentry waves you toward the largest tent. The sign above it reads: Captain Dunmere, Ridge Guard. The sign is spelled wrongly, and nobody has had time to fix it.
The courtyard is trampled to mud and bone-chips. Orcs lounge between stacked barrels, and they stop talking as you cross the threshold.
The largest of them rises from a throne made of three wagon seats lashed together. A greatsword the size of a door leans against his knee.
Hask paid for this yard. Hask paid in silver, and in the promise of a sunken city to loot. I do not know what you are, little glowing thing. But you will not walk through my gate.
Gorrak sinks to one knee and plants his sword in the mud. The orcs behind him drop their weapons, one by one, without being told.
Hask said the glow would pass to a worthy hand. I thought he lied. I was wrong. Go. The chapel door is not barred.
He pulls a tusk-shaped token from his belt and tosses it at your feet. Then he sits down heavily, and waves the rest of his warband away from the gate.
The chapel nave is hung with chains instead of banners. Where the altar stood, a table holds charts of the drowned coast, weighted with spent sunstone.
A tall man in a warden's coat, turned inside out, looks up from the charts. He has a pleasant face, and he smiles as if you were expected.
The lamp-bearer, at last. I have been counting the days. Shall we skip the speeches? I have a great many, and none of them will change how this ends.
You took the Sedge stone. You chained Greyfang. You emptied the Cinder Chapel. Why?
Because the sun sank, and someone ought to pull it back up. Come. Let me show you what I have learned.
Hask drops his cane and slides down the altar steps. The chains on the walls ring once, softly, like a struck bell.
Two shards of the dawn, you carry now. One in your palm, and one in that little piece of stone I let you have. There is a third, far south, with the Queen of the Dunes.
She is not my master. She is not yours either. She is only the one who is still awake.
His hand opens. A fragment of pale stone, warm as bread, rolls across the flagstones and stops against your boot.
He knew he'd lose. He wanted us to carry it south.
The camp is quiet when you come back down from the ridge. A hundred soldiers stand in rows, and nobody cheers.
Captain Ysra watches the chapel roof, where the gallows has been cut down. For the first time since you arrived, the wind is only wind.
Act one of the war is over. Whatever Hask was, we ended it here. But I read his charts. The road south goes through the Khesh Ura dunes, and there is a queen at the end of it.
The lamp in your palm pulses, once. It is pointing south.
